The saturation distance, which separates the weak and strong turbulence regimes, is given by z_s = [0.124 k^(7/6) C_n^2]^(-6/11).
The long-term lateral coherence length of a spherical wave, p_0(z), is considerably smaller than the aperture diameter for most cases of interest.
Under weak turbulence conditions, the 2-axis mean square wander angle of a transmitted laser beam is proportional to the integral of the aperture mutual coherence function M_δ(x) over the aperture.

Under strong turbulence conditions, the 2-axis mean square wander angle of a transmitted laser beam is proportional to the integral of x^(2/3) [1 - (Ex)^(5/3)] M_δ(x) exp[-2(Ex)^(5/3) z_s] over the aperture.
The correlation between the wander angle defined by the centroid and the tilt angle defined by a least-squares fit of the phase over the aperture is nearly 100% under weak turbulence conditions.

The engineering formula for the ratio of the peak on-axis transmitted intensity with tilt correction to the corresponding on-axis intensity in the absence of turbulence includes terms for atmospheric attenuation, the on-axis intensity in the absence of turbulence, and the turbulence strength and propagation range.
The index of refraction structure function, C_n^2, is modeled as a piecewise function of altitude, with different expressions for altitudes below and above 2000 meters.

The mean square wander angle of the transmitted laser beam and the tilt angle of the received spherical wave are approximately equal under strong turbulence conditions, differing by a numerical factor of order unity.
Tilt correction is of marginal benefit at best under strong turbulence conditions, as the laser beam breaks up into multiple patches or blobs rather than wandering as a whole.
The paper develops analytical expressions for the mean square wander angle of a transmitted laser beam and a received spherical wave under both weak and strong turbulence conditions.
The paper also analyzes the correlation between the wander angle defined by the centroid and the tilt angle defined by a least-squares fit of the phase over the aperture.
Engineering formulas are provided for calculating the peak on-axis transmitted intensity with tilt correction, which can be used for hand calculations.
The paper assumes a homogeneous-isotropic turbulent medium, with the index of refraction structure function, C_n^2, modeled as a function of altitude.
The results of the paper have implications for the effectiveness of adaptive optics systems in correcting for atmospheric turbulence effects on laser beams.
The paper demonstrates the transition from the weak turbulence regime, where the beam wanders as a whole, to the strong turbulence regime, where the beam breaks up into multiple patches or blobs.
